lessons.title: What motivates nursery workers
lessons.html:
Why motivation matters

Nursery work is repetitive: filling bags, sticking cuttings, weeding pots and moving trolleys day after day, often in heat or cold. A motivated team works carefully, notices problems and stays. A demotivated team makes mistakes, loses plants, takes more sick leave and leaves for other jobs. As supervisor you cannot control everything, but you have a big influence on how your team feels about their work.

Common motivators

  • Fair treatment: the same rules for everyone, no favourites.
  • Respect: greeting people, using their names, listening to their ideas.
  • Clear goals: knowing what is expected today and why it matters.
  • Recognition: being thanked and praised for good work.
  • Learning and growth: being trained in new tasks such as grafting or spraying, and having a chance of promotion.
  • Safe, decent conditions: protective clothing, clean toilets, drinking water, shade at break time.
  • Fair pay and benefits paid correctly and on time; these are set by management, but you can make sure hours are recorded correctly.

Common demotivators

  • Being shouted at or humiliated in front of others.
  • Unclear or constantly changing instructions.
  • Broken tools and missing materials that make the job harder.
  • Good work that is never noticed, while mistakes are always pointed out.
  • Unfair allocation of the worst tasks to the same people.

Knowing your people

Different people are motivated by different things. A young worker may want training and a path to supervisor; an experienced worker may value being asked for advice. Spend time talking to each team member, find out what they want, and notice changes in mood that may signal a problem at work or at home.

lessons.title: Practical ways to keep the team motivated
lessons.html:
Daily actions that build a strong team

Start the day well

Hold a short morning meeting of five to ten minutes. Greet everyone, explain the day's tasks and targets, mention any safety points, and share good news, such as a customer who was happy with an order of agapanthus. People work better when they understand the purpose of their task.

Set clear, achievable targets

Targets such as 1 200 cuttings stuck per person per day, or 400 bags potted before lunch, give people something to aim for. Targets must be realistic and agreed with the team, based on past performance. Show progress on a board in the potting shed so that everyone can see how the team is doing.

Recognise good work

  • Praise specific actions: You kept every label straight and the strike rate in your tray was the best this month.
  • Praise in public, correct in private.
  • Share credit with the team when the manager praises results.
  • Use any recognition schemes the nursery has, such as worker of the month.

Involve the team

Ask workers for ideas to improve a process. The people doing the work often know why the potting line keeps stopping. When an idea is used, say whose idea it was.

Share the work fairly

Rotate unpleasant tasks such as cleaning the chemical store or weeding in the heat. Rotating tasks also builds skills so that people can cover for each other.

Provide what they need

Make sure tools, materials and protective equipment are ready before work starts. Waiting around for potting mix or a working sprayer frustrates people and wastes time. Arrange drinking water and shade on hot days.

Develop people

Identify workers who want to learn and arrange on-the-job training or courses with the manager's approval. Growth gives people a reason to stay.

lessons.title: Dealing with low morale and measuring motivation
lessons.html:
When motivation drops

Signs of low morale include more late coming and absence, more mistakes and plant losses, workers arguing, slow work, complaints and people resigning. Do not ignore these signs.

Find the cause

  1. Look at what has changed: new targets, a new team member, overtime, hot weather, problems with pay.
  2. Talk to workers individually and in private. Ask open questions such as How is the work going for you? and listen without arguing.
  3. Separate issues you can solve from issues that belong to management.

Take action

  • Fix what is within your control quickly: repair tools, clarify instructions, rotate tasks.
  • Report issues you cannot solve, such as pay errors or transport problems, to the manager and give the team honest feedback on progress.
  • Never make promises you cannot keep, such as an increase you are not authorised to give.
  • If a worker has personal problems affecting their work, show care and refer them to any employee assistance or support the company offers.

Handling a difficult team member

One negative person can pull the whole team down. Speak to them privately about the specific behaviour, explain its effect on the team, agree on a change and follow up. If it continues, follow the company's disciplinary procedure with the manager.

Measuring motivation

You can track motivation through simple records: attendance and late coming, output against target, quality and losses, staff turnover and the number of improvement ideas. Look at the trend over weeks, not one bad day. Discuss the trends with your manager and plan improvements together.

Lead by example

The team copies the supervisor. Arrive on time, wear your protective equipment, work hard, stay calm under pressure and speak respectfully. Your attitude sets the tone for the whole nursery section.

Key points

  • Fairness, respect, clear goals, recognition and growth motivate people.
  • Hold short morning meetings and show progress against realistic targets.
  • Praise in public, correct in private, and share tasks fairly.
  • Look for the cause of low morale and act on what you can control.
  • Never make promises you are not authorised to keep.
  • Lead by example.

quiz.question: Which of these is most likely to demotivate a team?

options.text: Being shouted at in front of others

quiz.question: What is a good rule for giving feedback?

options.text: Correct in public, praise in private
Only give feedback once a year
Praise in public, correct in private
Never give praise so workers stay humble

quiz.question: How should production targets be set?

options.text: As high as possible, regardless of past performance
Realistic, agreed with the team and based on past performance

quiz.question: A worker complains that their pay is wrong. What should you do?

options.text: Report it to the manager and give the worker honest feedback on progress
Tell them it is not your problem
Pay them from your own pocket

options.text: To share the work fairly and build skills
To reduce the number of workers
